title: Study protocol for a non-randomized trial of community participation support for people with Acquired Brain Injury who have ceased driving in Japan
content:
by Satonori Nasu, Yu Ishibashi, Tsutomu Sasaki, Ryuji Kobayashi

Introduction

Driving cessation after acquired brain injury (ABI) represents a major life transition that can restrict community participation and negatively affect quality of life. Although many individuals are unable to resume driving after illness or injury, structured support programs addressing life after driving cessation remain limited, and prospective evaluations are scarce. This study protocol describes a theoretically grounded community life support program for individuals with ABI who have ceased driving.

Methods

This is a single-center, non-randomized controlled trial with ward-level cluster allocation conducted in a convalescent rehabilitation hospital in Japan. Participants with ABI who were determined to be unable to resume driving will be allocated at the ward level to either an intervention group receiving the Community Life Support Program for Individuals with Acquired Brain Injury after Driving Cessation (CLASP-AID) or a control group receiving usual care. CLASP-AID is a participant-centered program based on a person–occupation–environment framework and includes structured educational sessions for individuals and, when applicable, family members, information on alternative transportation, and training with alternative mobility devices. The primary outcome is occupational performance assessed using the Canadian Occupational Performance Measure, with the primary endpoint defined as the post-intervention COPM performance score. Secondary outcomes include readiness for mobility transition, health-related quality of life, depressive symptoms, environmental factors, and life-space mobility. The COPM, ARMT-J, SF-12, GDS-15, CEQ, and LSA will be assessed at baseline and post-intervention. When feasible, follow-up assessments will also be conducted at 1, 3, and 6 months after discharge to explore changes over time. LSA findings will be treated as exploratory because the baseline and post-intervention assessments are conducted during hospitalization and may be influenced by restrictions in life-space mobility associated with the inpatient environment.

Discussion

This study will provide insight into the potential associations of a structured, occupation-focused support program for individuals with ABI after driving cessation. The findings are expected to inform future intervention development and contribute to evidence-based strategies for supporting community participation following driving cessation.
